overview: This lesson introduces Class 4 students to the fascinating journey of water on Earth, known as the Water Cycle. Students will learn about the key processes of evaporation, condensation, and precipitation, understanding how water continuously moves from the Earth's surface to the sky and back again. We will also touch upon the role of oceans in this vital cycle.
objectives: [Remember] Identify evaporation, condensation, and precipitation as the main stages of the water cycle.
[Understand] Explain simply what happens during evaporation (water turning into vapour) and condensation (vapour forming tiny water droplets).
[Understand] Describe precipitation as water falling back to Earth in various forms.
[Apply] Give an example of evaporation or condensation from their daily life.
[Remember] State that the ocean covers a large part of Earth's surface (71%).

activities.title: Puddle Mystery
activities.description: Begin with a discussion. Ask students: 'What happens to puddles after it rains and the sun comes out?' or 'Where do you think rain comes from?' Encourage their ideas to set the stage for the water cycle concept.

activities.title: Water's Great Escape & Cloud Making
activities.description: Conduct a simple demonstration: place a wet sponge or cloth in sunlight or near a fan and observe it drying, explaining it as water 'escaping' into the air. Then, briefly explain how tiny water particles in the air form clouds. (No actual cloud making is needed, just a conceptual explanation).

activities.title: The Water Cycle Story
activities.description: Using a simplified diagram, the teacher will explain the main stages: Evaporation (water turning into vapour from oceans, lakes, and even land/plants – briefly mention transpiration). Condensation (vapour forming clouds). Precipitation (water falling back as rain). Emphasise the continuous nature of the cycle. Also, mention that oceans cover 71% of Earth's surface.

activities.title: My Water Cycle Observation
activities.description: Students share real-life examples where they might have seen parts of the water cycle, e.g., clothes drying on a line (evaporation), steam from a hot cup of tea (condensation forming tiny droplets), or dew on grass in the morning (condensation). Discuss why this cycle is important for us.

activities.title: Water Cycle Exit Ticket
activities.description: Students will quickly draw one stage of the water cycle they remember or write down one new word they learned about the water cycle on a small slip of paper before leaving the class.

assessment: Students' understanding will be checked through their participation in discussions, their ability to provide real-life examples of the water cycle, and their response on the 'Water Cycle Exit Ticket' (a quick drawing or written recall of a key term).
